title: Practice day: arrays and strings
overview: Module 10 is a practice day that brings together the two tools you have just learned, arrays and strings, and puts them to work on small judge problems. The five solutions here walk an array from both ends, treat a string as a plain character array, and check characters one by one. Everything uses only what the course has taught so far: loops, conditions, arrays and `scanf`/`printf` — no `<string.h>`, no functions of your own.

concepts.explain: To print an array in reverse, start the loop at the last index `n-1` and go down to `0`. Nothing needs to move in memory.
concepts.snippet: for(int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) printf("%d ", a[i]);

concepts.explain: Compare the first element with the last, the second with the second last, and keep moving towards the middle. One mismatch is enough to answer NO, so you can stop early.

concepts.term: A string is a char array ending in `'\0'`
concepts.explain: `scanf("%s", s)` fills the array and adds the null character at the end, and it stops at the first space. So the array must have one slot more than the longest word you expect.
Before `<string.h>` (Module 11) you find a length by walking the array until the closing `'\0'` and counting the steps. That loop is all `strlen` does.
concepts.snippet:
int length = 0;
for(int i = 0; s[i] != '\0'; i++) length++;

concepts.explain: Letters are stored as numbers (ASCII), and a capital letter is exactly 32 less than its small twin. So `s[i] - 32` makes a letter capital and `s[i] + 32` makes it small.
When a word is too long, print its first letter, then how many letters sit in the middle (`length - 2`), then its last letter.

files.title: Reversing: print an array backwards
files.what: Reads `n` numbers into an array and prints them in the opposite order. The statement forbids built-in functions, and none are needed: printing backwards is just a loop that counts down.
steps: Read `n`, then fill `a[0] … a[n-1]` with `scanf` inside a loop.
Start a second loop at `i = n - 1`, the last filled index, and run it down while `i >= 0`.
Print `a[i]` followed by a space on each step, so the numbers come out last-to-first.
The array itself is never changed: reversing the *printing* is enough, so no swapping and no second array are needed.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(n) for the array
files.input_note: The first example from the statement: `n = 4`, then the four values.
files.output_note: `2 3 1 5` — the input read right to left. The trailing space after the last number is fine; judges ignore spaces at the end of a line.
files.watch_out: Size the array by the constraint, not by the sample. `N` can reach 1000, so `a[1005]` is declared once and works for every test.

check.q: Why does the loop start at `n - 1` instead of `n`?
check.a: `n` values are stored at indices `0` to `n-1`, so `a[n]` is past the end. Starting at `n - 1` prints the last value first.

files.title: Palindrome Array: does it read the same both ways?
files.what: Prints YES when the array reads the same forwards and backwards, otherwise NO. It compares matching pairs from the two ends and stops as soon as a pair disagrees.
steps: Read `n` and fill the array.
Set a flag `is_palindrome = 1`, meaning "still a palindrome so far".
Loop `i` from `0` while `i < n / 2`, comparing `a[i]` with its mirror `a[n - 1 - i]`.
On the first mismatch set the flag to `0` and `break`: no later pair can repair it.
Print YES when the flag survived, otherwise NO.
Stopping at `n / 2` is enough because every pair is then checked once. With an odd `n` the middle element is skipped, and that is correct: it is its own mirror.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(n) for the array
files.input_note: The first example: five values that mirror around the middle `2`.
files.output_note: `YES`. The pairs (1,1) and (3,3) match and the middle `2` needs no partner. The second example `1 2 3 4` prints `NO`, because `1` and `4` differ immediately.
files.watch_out: Print exactly `YES` or `NO` in capitals; a judge compares the text character by character, so `Yes` fails.

check.q: With `n = 7`, how many comparisons does the loop make, and which element is never compared?
check.a: Three: (0,6), (1,5) and (2,4). The middle element at index 3 is skipped, because it mirrors onto itself.

files.title: Way Too Long Words: abbreviate words longer than 10

problem.name: Codeforces F - Way Too Long Words

files.what: For each of `t` words, prints the word unchanged when it is at most 10 characters, and otherwise the abbreviation: first letter, the number of letters in between, last letter.
steps: Read `t`, then repeat the whole job `t` times inside a loop.
Read one word with `scanf("%s", s)`, which stops at the space or newline and closes the word with `'\0'`.
Count the length by walking the array until that `'\0'`.
When the length is more than 10, print `s[0]`, then `length - 2`, then `s[length - 1]`.
Otherwise print the word as it is. Either way end the line with `\n`, because each test case needs its own line.
files.complexity: Time O(total characters) · Space O(1) beyond the word
files.input_note: The example from the statement: four words, one per line.
files.output_note: `word` is short, so it is printed unchanged. `localization` has 12 letters, giving `l` + 10 + `n` = `l10n`; `internationalization` gives `i18n`; the 45-letter word gives `p43s`.
files.watch_out: "Too long" means strictly more than 10, so a word of exactly 10 characters is printed unchanged. Using `>=` here is the classic wrong answer.

check.q: Why is the middle number `length - 2` and not `length`?
check.a: The first and last characters are printed as letters, so only the `length - 2` characters between them are counted.

files.title: Conversion: swap letter case and turn commas into spaces
files.what: Reads one string and prints it character by character: every comma becomes a space, every small letter becomes capital and every capital becomes small.
steps: Read the string with `scanf("%s", s)`. This is safe here because the input holds only letters and commas, never a space.
Walk the array with a loop that runs while `s[i] != '\0'`.
When the character is a comma, print a space instead.
When it is between `'a'` and `'z'`, print `s[i] - 32`, which is the same letter in capitals.
Otherwise it is a capital letter, so print `s[i] + 32` to make it small.
Nothing is stored back into the array: each character is decided and printed as it is met.
files.complexity: Time O(|S|) · Space O(|S|) for the string
files.input_note: The example from the statement: one line, letters and commas only.
files.output_note: `HAPPY nEWyEAR ENJOY` — both commas became spaces, `happy` became capitals, and in `NewYear` each letter flipped the other way.
files.watch_out: `scanf("%s", ...)` stops at the first space, so it only works because this input has no spaces. The spaces appear in the *output*, which is printed one character at a time.

check.a: In ASCII the capital letters sit 32 places before the small ones (`'A'` is 65, `'a'` is 97), so the same shift works for every letter.

files.title: Strings: sizes, joining, and swapping first letters
files.what: Reads two words and prints three lines: their two lengths, the two words joined together, and the two words again after their first characters have traded places.
steps: Read both words into `a` and `b` with `scanf("%s", ...)`.
Count each length with its own loop that stops at `'\0'`, then print them separated by a space.
For the join, print `a` and then `b` with nothing in between: `printf("%s%s\n", a, b)` gives `A + B` without building a third array.
Swap the first characters through a temporary variable: keep `a[0]` in `temp`, copy `b[0]` into `a[0]`, then put `temp` into `b[0]`.
Print both words again, now separated by a single space.
files.input_note: The example from the statement: `A` on the first line, `B` on the second.
files.output_note: `4 2` are the two lengths; `abcdef` is the join; `ebcd af` is the pair after the first letters traded places — `abcd` starts with `e` and `ef` starts with `a`.
files.watch_out: The swap needs the temporary variable. Writing `a[0] = b[0]` first would overwrite `a[0]`, and `b[0]` would then be given its own value back.

check.q: Why can the second line be printed without making a new array?
check.a: Concatenation only matters for what is shown. Printing `a` immediately followed by `b` puts the same characters on the line, in the same order.

practice_links.name: Strings (ignore the Note section of the statement)

recap: Reverse output needs no swapping: just loop from `n-1` down to `0`.
A palindrome check compares matching pairs from both ends and stops at the middle.
Strings are char arrays that end with `'\0'`; before Module 10 is over you count a length with a loop, not with `strlen`.
Characters are small numbers: a capital letter is 32 less than its small twin.
Swapping two values always needs a temporary variable.
Read the output format closely: spaces, new lines and case all matter on a judge.

check_yourself.q: For `n = 6`, which index pairs does a palindrome check compare?
check_yourself.a: (0,5), (1,4) and (2,3). The loop stops once `i` reaches `n / 2`, when every pair has been seen.

check_yourself.q: What does `'d' - 'a'` evaluate to, and why is that useful?
check_yourself.a: 3. It turns a letter into a 0-based position, which you can use as an array index.

check_yourself.q: Why must a string array be at least one longer than the longest word?
check_yourself.a: The extra slot holds the `'\0'` that marks the end of the string.

check_yourself.q: `scanf("%s", s)` reads `happy new year` into `s`. What does `s` hold?
check_yourself.a: Only `happy`. `%s` stops at the first space, which is why it works for the Conversion problem, where the input has no spaces.
